description: A hackathon focused on leveraging NASA data to transform agriculture by developing innovative solutions that help farmers make better decisions.
summary:
SOWSCOPE helps farmers compare crop-rotation plans for Story County, Iowa. A user builds two crop sequences from corn, soybean, alfalfa and oats, and sees them side by side. The comparison shows growing seasons, different crops, crop changes and repeated crops. It shows counts only, with no score and no ranking, so the farmer decides.

The app displays NASA POWER weather summaries and ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 soil estimates for the Story County reference point, with their sources and limits shown. Rotation decisions affect soil and later harvests, but the trade-offs are hard to compare by hand. SOWSCOPE makes them visible.

It does not predict yields or assess field-level effects. The next step is a guide that compares proposals with past-year trends, with confidence levels.
details:
SOWSCOPE

Field Shifting and Crop Rotation with NASA Data

NASA Space Apps 2026  ·  Story County, Iowa  ·  Project documentation

1. Project Summary

SOWSCOPE helps a farmer compare two crop-rotation plans for Story County, Iowa. The farmer sees the structure of both plans side by side, with the climate and soil context for the same location, and then decides.

The problem

·        Farmers find it hard to choose which crop to plant on a field, and when to move crops to another field (crop rotation and field shifting).

·        Poor choices lead to low production and exhausted soil.

Why it matters

·        Shows which crops suit a plot and prolongs the useful life of the land.

·        Supports soil conservation and optimum production.

2. What the Project Does

The user selects Iowa and builds two scenarios from four crops: corn, soybean, alfalfa and oats. Each scenario is shuffled or set in a chosen order. The app then compares the two on:

·        number of growing seasons

·        crops used

·        how often crops change from one season to the next

·        where crops repeat

The comparison gives counts only. It does not score or rank the scenarios, so the farmer chooses.

Current limits. Iowa is the only working region, and the crop list is fixed to the four major crops (cereal rye is available as a cover crop).

3. How It Works, Step by Step

The app is used in this order: sign up, read the dashboard, explore the location, build scenarios in the Rotation Planner, compare them, and check the data sources. The screenshots below follow that order.

Step 4: Rotation Planner

The Rotation Planner is the core of the app. The user builds up to two scenarios (more can be added, up to four) and chooses how each sequence is made. There are two functions:

·        Function 1: Shuffle. The app randomly orders the chosen crops and explains the sequence.

·        Function 2: Compare. The user sets the order of each scenario by hand, then compares the two (see Step 4b).

Step 5: Data & Methodology

This section explains where every number comes from and how far it can be trusted.

What happens here:

·        A banner reads Story County data ready: NASA POWER weather and SoilGrids estimates for the project location.

·        Value Provenance sorts every value into one of four types: Measured (none: no ground measurements are included), Modelled (SoilGrids soil values for 0–5 cm), Derived (monthly and sequence summaries from NASA POWER and the entered sequences), and Assumed (none: the app assumes no yield, profit or crop performance).

What happens here:

·        The source register lists ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 (clay, nitrogen, pH and organic carbon; modelled estimates; Loaded) and NASA GPM IMERG (precipitation comparison; a potential future source; Not available).

6. How the Comparison Is Calculated

SOWSCOPE compares two user-defined crop sequences using descriptive counts. It does not calculate yield, profitability, nitrogen credits, or an overall score that identifies a winning rotation.

Metric

How it is calculated

Growing seasons

Count the number of entries in each crop sequence.

Different crops

Count the distinct crop types in the sequence.

Crop changes

Count consecutive season-to-season transitions where the crop changes.

Repeated crops

Count each time a crop appears again after its first appearance in the sequence.

 

Worked example. Scenario A: Corn → Soybean → Alfalfa → Alfalfa. It has 4 growing seasons and 3 distinct crops. Its transitions are Corn → Soybean (change), Soybean → Alfalfa (change) and Alfalfa → Alfalfa (no change, repeat). Result: 2 crop changes, 1 repeat.

7. Benefits

·        Farmers and advisers see the structure of two rotation plans in one view, instead of working it out season by season.

·        Climate and soil context for the same location sits beside the comparison.

·        Each data value is labelled with its source, period and limits, so users know what it can and cannot show.

8. Intended Impact

·        Make rotation planning more transparent and encourage soil-conscious choices.

·        Support the farmer's own judgement and agronomists' advice, not replace them.

·        Next stage: a guide that compares each proposal with past-year trends, with a confidence level on every estimate.

·        Long-term aim: help farmers plan for changing conditions.

9. How the Project Is Creative

·        Brings together satellite and climate data with practical agronomic knowledge, which are usually kept apart.

·        Does not turn uncertain research into a score. It shows where the evidence applies and where it does not.

·        The decision stays with the user.

10. Factors the Team Considered

·        Local context: research and data from one place are not assumed to apply to another, so the app is limited to Story County.

·        Data reliability: each source is checked for coverage, resolution and what it can and cannot show.

·        Scientific uncertainty: where evidence is incomplete, the app says so instead of producing unsupported numbers.

·        Limits on predictions: the app does not estimate yields or field-level effects, because it lacks the data to do so reliably.

·        Usability: results are presented so farmers can read them without specialist training.

11. Challenges and Solutions

Finding the right data

Many sources were needed, and some required data was not provided. The team used NASA and ISRIC data portals and API documentation to retrieve the datasets, plus open dataset search tools (Kaggle, Google Dataset Search) to fill gaps.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Unstable internet

Most of the work was online, and the campus Wi-Fi was unstable, so the team used its own connection.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Understanding the project scope

At the start the team found the expectations hard to decode. Thorough research and information gathering resolved this.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Materialization

Building the app was resolved quickly by agreeing on the programming language early.

12. Conclusion

SOWSCOPE does not replace farmers' experience. It supports decision making by showing the possible crop-rotation scenarios and how they affect field shifting.
